items.title: GOP Congressman in California Swing-District Race Defends Vote for Medicaid Cuts
items.summary: In a race that could help decide control of Congress, Republican U.S. Rep. David Valadao is trying to hold on to his swing-district seat. The congressman didn’t mention healthcare at a recent campaign rally in Bakersfield, but voters can't stop talking about it.
items.author: Jackie Fortiér
items.full_html:
BAKERSFIELD, Calif. — Ulises Hernandez has had health coverage through Medicaid for as long as he can remember. But he had never waited as long for care as he did in September after a dental crown slipped down his throat during a procedure. He spent eight hours in an emergency room waiting for care and more than two days without food.

Sitting in his wheelchair to protest looming federal Medicaid cuts outside Republican U.S. Rep. David Valadao’s Bakersfield office, Hernandez described his wait as a foreshadowing of what’s ahead.

“I couldn’t eat, I couldn’t drink, I couldn’t do anything, and I was in pain,” said Hernandez, who had been discharged from the hospital a few days before. “I’m livid.”

Hernandez, 41, said Valadao “should be ashamed of himself” for voting for the Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The law is expected to reduce Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion through 2034, with provisions such as stricter Medicaid eligibility rules and reducing federal money to states.

Hernandez plans to vote for challenger Randy Villegas in hopes that this Central Valley toss-up district, where roughly 6 in 10 of constituents are enrolled in Medicaid, can help give Democrats control of Congress.

Villegas, a political science professor, has embraced the progressive rallying cry for “Medicare for All” and called out Valadao for a vote “that is going to rip away healthcare from Valley families,” since many working-age adults may not satisfy new work requirements and twice-a-year eligibility checks that, by political design, start after the midterm elections.

Valadao defends his vote on the GOP bill. During a televised Oct. 6 debate, he said “there are no actual cuts” to Medicaid.

An estimated 60,000 more residents of his district could be without coverage by 2034 due to the tax and spending bill and the expiration of enhanced premium tax credits for Affordable Care Act insurance plans, according to the left-leaning Center for American Progress think tank.

Researchers estimate that those new rules will push more than 2 million Californians statewide off their coverage and that the state stands to lose about $30 billion a year, more than any other state.

Fertile Ground, High Unemployment

Bakersfield is an oil town, and it wears that identity proudly. Pump jacks nod in the distance. Streets run wide. The Kern River’s bed lies dry, its water siphoned to feed the agricultural fields. Sitting partially in the southernmost portion of the contested congressional district, this city produces much from the land, but unemployment is high.

Democrats have outnumbered Republicans in voter registrations by double-digit percentage points in Valadao’s district since he was first elected to the U.S. House in 2012, yet he has won six of his seven congressional elections. He has survived by focusing on local issues such as water infrastructure and distancing himself from the Trump administration, said Jeffrey Cummins, a political science professor at California State University-Fresno. Valadao is the last Republican House incumbent who voted to impeach Trump after the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol who is running for reelection to Congress.

“This is an area where, even when we see the registration advantage for Democrats, that they are moderate Democrats who tend to be concerned with agricultural issues, and Valadao in the past has successfully appeased those voters,” Cummins said.

But California’s congressional map was redrawn last year as part of a national mid-decade redistricting fight, and Valadao’s Central Valley seat is considered more favorable for Democrats than before. Cummins said a different mix of voters, coupled with anger toward incumbents, could flip the seat.

“Valadao knows that he’s on notice,” Cummins said.

Nationwide, healthcare costs remain a top affordability concern for voters, and they trust Democrats over Republicans by a 2-to-1 margin on the issue, according to a September KFF poll. Valadao lost in 2018, when Democrats targeted his votes to repeal the ACA, as well as his alliance with Trump. On Nov. 3, he faces Villegas, a populist backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) who favors a single-payer universal healthcare system.

“The system that we have now, we pay twice as much as other countries across the world, despite the fact that we have worse healthcare outcomes,” Villegas said during the debate.

No Mention of Healthcare

Valadao participated in a $1,000-a-ticket fundraiser on Sept. 30. He was joined by House Speaker Mike Johnson, who is campaigning across 22 states in six weeks as Republicans try to hold the chamber. Afterward, press were allowed at an invitation-only reelection event in Bakersfield, held in an office building just outside of the new district Valadao hopes to represent. Arches of red, white, and blue star-shaped balloons framed the small stage.

Neither lawmaker mentioned Medicaid or the rising cost of healthcare when they spoke to the audience. After brief speeches, Valadao repeatedly refused to answer KFF Health News’ questions about his vote for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and its impact on his constituents’ Medicaid coverage, saying, “I think you are distorting the truth.”

Of the half dozen attendees KFF Health News approached among roughly 50 in the room, none lived in Valadao’s district.

They came anyway. Retired nurse Charlotte Brandt lives in the neighboring Republican-held district but follows Valadao’s votes closely. She called him “a hero for the Central Valley,” citing his work on water, oil, and agriculture, which she said sustain Kern County as the “breadbasket of the world.”

Her daughter, Allison Brandt Oliver, who also lives in Republican Vince Fong’s district, said she favored the stricter Medicaid eligibility rules Republicans put into place, saying her concern is whether spending is going to U.S. citizens who contribute to the economy.

A few days later during the televised debate, Valadao said he was among the negotiators who secured community engagement provisions in the law, which will require certain adults to prove they’re working or completing other activities such as job training or volunteering.

“It’s not an actual cut,” Valadao said. “We need people to actually put in and make a fair effort to try to cover their expenses and be a part of their community. This is not an unreasonable ask.”

Millions in Ads, One Swing Seat

In a sign of how vital this district is, Republicans and Democrats had each booked more than $16 million in ads here through Election Day, according to data compiled by AdImpact.

“When you start getting over $10 million of spending total in the district, I would say that that’s pretty high,” Cummins said.

Some of the ads are reaching voters in unexpected ways.

Outside a local library, Seslie Maese, a stay-at-home mom from Bakersfield, said her 7-year-old, who often watches Lego videos on YouTube, runs to her whenever a certain ad plays. “David Valadago is going on vacation again, Mom,” he announces, mispronouncing the congressman’s name. Her son doesn’t realize the ad, paid for by a Democratic political action committee, means that as a criticism.

Maese is undecided. Even though she’s a registered Republican, she said what she has heard about Valadao doesn’t sound positive, such as that he went back on his pledge not to cut Medicaid for vulnerable populations by voting for the federal tax-and-spending law.

For Maese, a politician who says one thing and does another is a deal-breaker.

“He just hasn’t come through with anything he said,” she said, “especially since he cut off a lot of Medicaid.”

items.title: Shopping for an ACA Plan This Year? Here’s What You Need To Know
items.summary: As open enrollment for Affordable Care Act health insurance kicks off, consumers face rising premiums, additional identity checks, and fewer brokers.
items.author: Julie Appleby
items.full_html:
Consumers who buy Affordable Care Act health insurance are going to see changes both big and small as open enrollment for 2027 coverage kicks off. These include premium increases, possible additional identity checks, potential delays in working with a broker, and new limits on which immigrants can get subsidies.

Shoppers need to plan accordingly.

Open enrollment starts Nov. 1 in most states. Idaho, Connecticut, and Massachusetts start earlier, and some states are already allowing “window shopping” to check premium rates.

A continued decline in overall enrollment is expected, mainly because of the expiration of enhanced subsidies at the end of 2025. Policy experts say the end of those subsidies led millions to drop or lose coverage through the first few months of this year.

But the Trump administration sees victory in the falling enrollment, crediting its various efforts to reduce fraud, including the August cancellation of policies covering 760,000 enrollees suspected to be improperly signed up. A small number of those enrollees have regained coverage.

Have Your ID Ready

One of the biggest changes will be increased scrutiny of both consumers and agents via requirements aimed at thwarting fraud or improper enrollments. For consumers, it could slow the enrollment process.

The new rules, outlined in a Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services FAQ, affect only consumers using agents or brokers to help them enroll through the federal marketplace, which serves 29 states. They do not apply to state-based exchanges, which have their own rules and have in most cases been more successful at preventing fraudulent sign-ups.

For starters, all consumers using an agent in the federal marketplace will need to get a one-time confirmation code or link to authorize a specific agent to enroll them or make changes on their behalf. It will be sent to consumers by text message, email, or an automated phone call from one of the private enrollment platforms used by their agent. Returning consumers who have incorrect or outdated contact information will first need to call the federal marketplace themselves or submit an application online to update it.

Additionally, consumers and policyholders deemed “high-risk” must verify their own identity before authorizing an agent. CMS defines as “high-risk” first-time applicants or those with existing coverage whose applications involve a change of state, as well as consumers working with a new or different agent or with a monthly premium payment of $30 or less.

Joshua Brooker, who oversees an insurance agency in Pennsylvania, said CMS appears to have selected people in those groups for greater scrutiny because “someone who is moving to a new state or switching brokers — that could be a broker trying to impersonate a consumer.”

The $30-a-month cutoff may be tied to concerns that plans with no or low monthly premiums are easier for bad agents to target for unauthorized enrollments because the policyholder may never get a bill. Some rogue agents even pay the low monthly amount themselves and still make a profit from the commission, Brooker said.

The broad nature of the new rules, though, has Brooker concerned “that up to 1 in 5 consumers is going to have to do extra identity proofing” and may just give up and not get insured.

Consumers designated high-risk must prove their identity through a CMS-approved third party such as credit company Experian, which generally asks questions only the consumer should be able to answer. People who fail this test may be asked to call Experian’s help desk or submit their applications themselves by creating a healthcare.gov account, which requires them to upload identification such as a driver’s license, a passport, immigration papers, or another form of ID.

“Some people may have trouble not because they’re not real, but because they don’t have a credit file, or have moved, or have changed names,” said Stacey Pogue, a senior research fellow at the Center on Health Insurance Reforms at Georgetown University.

She said the changes might “be an appropriate response by CMS that targets fraudulent enrollments but might also create extra hurdles.”

There May Be Fewer Brokers

CMS in September issued a rule that places a moratorium on brokers new to offering ACA coverage. Agents not registered with the federal marketplace in 2026 will not be allowed to assist with enrollments for 2027 until February at the earliest, past the end of open enrollment season.

CMS said it took this step because a disproportionate number of “significant compliance concerns” in 2026 came from newly registered agents or brokers. Additionally, the agency has kicked out “hundreds of non-compliant agents and brokers” this year.

Jason Fine, who runs a brokerage in Florida, said he agrees with the concept behind these changes. He has reported multiple times to CMS, for instance, that rogue agents have switched his clients’ coverage without authorization, wanting the agency to take action against them. But he said the updated rules also raise concerns.

“Everything they are doing in the long term makes sense,” he said. However, in the short term, “I don’t know if they care about the chaos it will cause.”

That’s because the moratorium will make it much harder for small brokers to help clients this year. His agency and others often pare their staffing after open enrollment but hire again toward the end of the year. He was planning to add up to 10 agents to his core staff of about five but has been told by recruiters that he’s unlikely to be able to find anyone who was registered for 2026 and is still available.

He suggested that the move unintentionally benefits larger call centers, some of which were doing much of the marketing that regulators feared led to unauthorized switching. Call centers often maintain larger staffs.

“They can afford to keep a staff of 25 or 40 people all year long,” Fine said.

Groups representing agents are very unhappy with the directive. One, the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals, filed a lawsuit Oct. 15 against the Trump administration over the moratorium, saying it unfairly targets 19,000 agents who may want to sell ACA plans for next year.

“Just because you’re a new agent doesn’t mean you are fraudulent,” said Ronnell Nolan, president of Health Agents for America, another sales agent group, which on Oct. 21 filed suit seeking a temporary restraining order on the moratorium. “All these agencies who have trained new agents and paid thousands of dollars now have people who won’t be able to work.”

It all leads to an important piece of advice from Georgetown’s Pogue: Consumers should not delay making appointments. “If you rely on an agent or broker, and a lot of people do, their slots might fill up faster because there will be fewer of them to help with enrollment. I would reach out early.”

Costs Will Continue To Be an Issue

This year, after Congress did not renew the expiring enhanced subsidies, most people getting ACA coverage saw what they had to pay increase. Higher earners lost subsidies entirely. Add in double-digit premium increases, and most people had to pay substantially more for their coverage.

But most people who buy ACA coverage for next year will still receive a subsidy. It will just be less generous than it was before the enhancements expired at the end of 2025.

The subsidies are pegged to the premium costs of benchmark plans, the name given to the second-lowest-price silver-tier plan in an area.

This helps offset premium increases.

“For most folks, overall affordability will stay about the same,” said Louise Norris, a health policy analyst for HealthInsurance.org. “That’s not to say it’s great, but if you were able to manage the premiums this year, it should be similar to that.”

But there are other factors at work, too.

Last year’s average premium increase of 26% was the largest in years. It was driven in part by insurers’ fear that the expiration of subsidies would cause healthier people to drop out of the marketplace. Other drivers often cited for such increases include a rise in overall medical care costs, inflation, and labor shortages.

For the upcoming year, those dynamics remain a concern, with premiums slated for double-digit increases, although, at 15%, slightly lower than last year.

Subsidies are income-based and cut off for households earning more than four times the federal poverty rate. During this open enrollment season, that amount is $63,840 for a single person, $86,560 for a couple, and $109,280 for a family of three, for example.

“The biggest issue we will face is affordability,” said Anne Petry, who, with her father, owns Jaggi Petry Insurance & Investments in Forsyth, Illinois, and helps customers purchase health insurance, including ACA plans. “There definitely will come a breaking point for people.”

Agents and other experts say consumers should not allow their plans to automatically renew and should instead go online to compare premiums and coverage, which can change each year even for the same plan. There may be less expensive alternatives, including plans from new insurers, so they suggest looking at not just premiums, but also deductibles and other costs. At the same time, several insurers, including Cigna, have dropped all or part of their ACA coverage areas.

“If you just sit on the sidelines and let the policy auto-renew, you might miss out on what could be a better opportunity,” Norris said. She said it is important to check options because the cap on out-of-pocket maximums for ACA plans is also increasing.

That amount, which represents the most a consumer must pay toward deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance before the policy is expected to cover remaining in-network medical costs, was $10,600 for an individual and $21,200 for a family plan this year. In 2027, it will grow by 13% to $12,000 for an individual and $24,000 for family coverage. Lower caps on out-of-pocket maximums are set for households earning up to 2.5 times the federal poverty level.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Congress passed last year, also strips subsidy eligibility from many lawfully present immigrants, including people holding temporary H-1B work visas, refugees, asylees, people with temporary protected status, and those with pending green-card applications.

Three immigrant groups can still get ACA subsidies: green-card holders, who have permanent legal status; certain Cuban and Haitian immigrants; and citizens of Micronesia, the Marshall Islands, or Palau.

Members of the media are invited to join NASA at the 2026 von Braun Space Exploration Symposium from Monday, Oct. 26, to Wednesday, Oct. 28, at the University of Alabama in Huntsville.

This year’s symposium is focused on humanity’s return to the Moon, sustainable lunar infrastructure, advanced space propulsion, and the evolving space workforce.

Panels include discussions on Artemis II and III, space propulsion flash talks, building utilities and infrastructure for sustainable lunar operations, Moon base supply chain resilience, space nuclear technology, navigating the new NASA workforce, and engineering the future, featuring keynotes and awards presentations.

  • Deputy Associate Administrator Casey Swails
  • Stephen Cash, director, NASA Marshall
  • Nicky Fox, associate administrator, Science Mission Directorate, NASA Headquarters
  • Charlie Blackwell-Thompson, Artemis II launch director, NASA Kennedy
  • Steve Creech, Human Landing System program manager, NASA Marshall
  • Debbie Whitis Korth, acting program manager, Orion Program, NASA Johnson

To request an interview with NASA speakers during the event, media must contact Lance D. Davis, lance.d.davis@nasa.gov, and Joel Wallace, joel.w.wallace@nasa.gov. Media interested in participating in-person or online must contact the American Astronomical Society to register.

Organized by the American Astronautical Society in collaboration with NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, the annual event gathers leaders from government, industry, policy, and academia to discuss the current landscape of space exploration and help chart a path forward.

items.title: Job-Based Health Plan Costs Rise, With Little Relief in Sight
items.summary: Employers saw their healthcare premiums rise 5% this year — and some passed on that burden to workers — as the cost of family coverage in job-based insurance exceeds $28,000 for family plans.
items.author: Julie Appleby
items.full_html:
Rising healthcare costs aren’t a problem just for those who buy their own health insurance. Increases hit employers and their workers this year, too, and more are expected for 2027 plans — adding to growing concerns about affordability heading into the midterm elections.

Polls show that healthcare costs — and affordability, in general — are among top concerns cited by likely voters. Much attention has been focused on mounting costs and declining enrollment in Affordable Care Act plans, the insurance used by roughly 19 million people who buy their own. But work-based plans are adding financial pressure for the more than 150 million Americans covered through their jobs.

One of the biggest changes this year, for instance, came in the amount workers pay toward their own coverage, rising an average of 9% to $7,471 annually for a family, according to a broad annual survey released Oct. 22 by KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. That’s up from the 7.6% jump seen from 2024 to 2025.

Their employers, too, faced additional costs, with the average family coverage premium rising 5% to hit $28,303, according to the survey.

In response to that increase — which comes on the heels of a 6% increase the previous year — 44% of large employers, with at least 200 employees, said they upped what workers had to pay toward coverage.

“When we start to see higher use or higher prices, there are only a limited number of things employers can do” to try to slow premium increases, said Matthew Rae, associate director of the Program on the Health Care Marketplace at KFF.

Employers reported taking other actions in the past year to hold down their costs, such as increasing deductibles (the amounts people pay toward their care before insurance pitches in), changing insurers, adding preapproval for some services, or offering workers a narrower choice of healthcare providers, the KFF report said.

Workers’ earnings rose an average of 3.7% this year, the survey found, while overall inflation was 2.7%.

People who work for small companies, with fewer than 200 employees, paid more for healthcare than their counterparts at larger companies.

For example, health plans at large companies had a $1,772 average annual deductible for an individual employee, while small workplaces averaged $2,624.

Overall, though, the share workers pay toward the total premium across all companies ticked up only slightly from the previous year, hitting 27% of the cost for family coverage and 18% for individual coverage, with employers picking up the remainder.

Driving Up Costs

Other groups have recently posted projections of what employers might face next year.

Consulting firm AON, for example, projected employers could pay 9.5% more next year, the fourth consecutive year of big increases, while a similar company, Marsh, estimated 8.2%, the highest jump since 2003. Costs are going up for many reasons, from people utilizing more services to skyrocketing prices of prescription drugs and rapidly rising hospital prices, the reports say.

Also helping drive up costs is artificial intelligence, say other reports, including one from the Business Group on Health, a membership organization of self-insured employers. The report said hospital systems and other medical providers use the technology to maximize insurer and patient billing.

The business group predicted a median premium increase of 9.2% next year, although employers might reduce that by making benefit changes.

Until recently, employers absorbed the lion’s share of cost increases, “but that’s starting to change a bit,” said Jim Winkler, chief strategy officer for the group. “When open enrollment starts, most people will see their out-of-paycheck costs and probably their out-of-pocket costs going up.”

Looking ahead, the group suggests employers take further action to forestall increases in 2028, Winkler said. One idea is to offer lower copayments for some health providers based on their prices or quality, similar to “tiered networks,” a strategy employers and insurers have tried, with only 4% of companies sticking with it, according to the KFF survey. “What’s old is new again,” Winkler noted, saying it might work better now because it’s easier than ever for apps to show consumers the providers with the lowest copayments, which would be set by an employer or insurer.

Overlooked in much of the discussion on rising health costs, said Elizabeth Mitchell, president and CEO of the large employer organization Purchaser Business Group on Health, is the role played by the healthcare industry — from hospitals to drugmakers to insurers.

She asked: Why are the customers — the employers, in this case — being asked what they are doing about it? “The industry is doing absolutely nothing to control costs, as evidenced by the relentless growth in costs,” she said.

Businesses are using new pricing information made available under federal rules to contract directly in some cases with hospitals and other providers and to invest in primary care.

Mitchell and others say Congress should also get involved. Health policy researchers at Georgetown University, for example, suggest capping annual deductibles, setting hospital price caps, and extending lower drug prices negotiated by Medicare to the private sector.

Keeping Costs Flat

Not all companies saw an increase this year.

Take KFF survey respondent Phifer Inc., a company based in Tuscaloosa, Alabama, that makes insect screens and precision woven products, such as outdoor furniture fabric. Its health costs remained flat this year, likely because it has put a strong focus in recent years on providing zero-cost primary care to its workers through on-site clinics and direct contracts with doctors’ offices, said Russell DuBose, the company’s vice president of human resources.

Only 7% of companies in the KFF survey reported having an on-site clinic, although 24% said they had one on-site or nearby.

Workers get in quickly to see a primary care doctor, DuBose said, and that can help with both prevention of disease and catching problems early. The company also directly contracts with other types of specialists.

“We steer plan members to the best providers that we can find,” DuBose said. “When we do that, we’re paying a more reasonable price.”

The company is self-insured, like many employers. That means it pays all the bills itself and buys what’s called stop-loss insurance to help with very high bills. That coverage has also jumped in price, DuBose said.

He often gets calls from other employers asking about his company’s strategy — and how to control costs. Now, far more so than in recent years, he said, employers are nervous, worried about costs continuing to rise and what that would mean.

“The worry is ‘Could the rising cost of healthcare be the next job killer?’” he said.

Among other findings from the annual KFF report:

  • Twenty-nine percent of all companies surveyed said covering GLP-1s, a new class of weight loss drug, had a “significant” effect on their drug costs.
  • Many companies — about 29% of large ones — reported difficulty getting information on how much their plans paid for medical care or price comparisons among providers.
  • About 9% of companies with 50 or more workers buy prescription drugs from outside the U.S. to save money.

items.title: Trump Dangles Rural Health Dollars To Push States To Change Hospital Laws
items.summary: The Trump administration has tied billions in rural health funding for states partly to the policy commitments they make, including ending their certificate of need, or CON, laws governing the construction of new hospitals.
items.author: Andrew Jones
items.full_html:
The Trump administration has hinged federal funding for states on whether they end or loosen powerful but controversial laws that regulate the construction of new hospitals — with a handful of states poised to comply.

A chunk of the $50 billion available to states through the five-year Rural Health Transformation Program is partly contingent on policy commitments. The administration told states it would score their applications higher if they walked back their certificate of need, or CON, laws, which give a state approval authority over the expansion or construction of any healthcare facility. Six states indicated plans to revisit their laws in their applications.

Certificate of need laws, which require that a healthcare provider prove a community need for a new service, were intended to curb monopolies and rising costs. But critics of the laws say they’ve instead raised healthcare prices, stalled needed facilities, and barred rural patients from new technology. More than 30 states, plus Washington, D.C., enforce some sort of certificate of need law, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

Legislators in several states have been pushing to end the laws, which have faced scrutiny for decades — under Republican and Democratic administrations. But the Trump administration’s aggressive approach to tie the policies to funding has forced states to reckon with their laws quickly.

The Rural Health Transformation Program was added to President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act as an initiative to modernize healthcare in remote areas. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, in its notice to states applying to the program, called certificate of need laws “an additional expense and burden on rural facilities” and explained how states with fewer certificate of need rules would get higher scores.

“It’s not the first time the federal government used funding as a state carrot (versus using a stick) to encourage alignment on an administration’s policy goal,” Maureen Hensley-Quinn, a researcher at the National Academy for State Health Policy, said in an email. She noted that President Barack Obama’s administration included millions of dollars in performance bonuses for states that made it easier for children to enroll in federally funded health insurance.

Hensley-Quinn said the funding “carrot” was an opportunity to take a hard look at whether policies like certificates of need were truly worth it.

“States need to carefully weigh the trade-offs of supporting a ‘voluntary’ federal policy no matter what,” she said, “and additional federal financing, especially in tight state budget years, can tip the scale.”

Obama, Trump on Same Page

Since the Rural Health Transformation Program became law last year, Tennessee has taken the most concrete action. In a bipartisan vote in April, state lawmakers passed a bill that will unravel most of its remaining certificate of need rules over the next four years. Alaska, Connecticut, Delaware, Iowa, and Mississippi have also said they would consider ending or loosening their laws.

“If there’s an issue where you can have President Obama and President Trump in agreement on something, that tells you the idea probably has some merit,” Wes Climer, a Republican state senator in South Carolina, said in 2021, supporting the repeal of that state’s certificate of need law. The legislature voted in 2023 to end most rules in the law, and in January it will stop requiring certificate of need applications for new hospital construction or expansion, leaving them only for nursing homes.

Some certificate of need laws require approval for changes as minor as a new piece of expensive equipment. In North Carolina, a hospital that won a certificate of need to build a much-needed facility was mired in a court battle for three years before breaking ground in 2026.

As more states consider removing their certificate of need laws, Hensley-Quinn warns of unintended consequences: Fewer records will exist that help states track hospital ownership.

Hensley-Quinn said frustrated state officials have come to her years after their states repealed certificate of need laws, saying that even with a licensure process, they don’t have insight into the financial state of their health systems or facilities, or how they’re managed. Certificate of need laws force companies seeking a new foothold in the state to submit voluminous applications. Once the laws are gone, few regulations force transparency. That leaves states unaware when a health system contracts with private equity to provide hospital services, for example.

“Without CON, without ownership reporting, and without an entity that monitors transactions or providers in that way, there’s no way for you to know,” Hensley-Quinn said.

Tennessee’s Certificate of Need Law

Tennessee lawmakers had pushed to change the state’s certificate of need law for years but didn’t pass sweeping legislation until it faced losing out on federal funding. Like all states, Tennessee is set to receive an equal share of half of the Rural Health Transformation Program’s grants, while the other $25 billion in funding is contingent on other factors, including states’ policy commitments.

In 2024, the state’s hospital association opposed a repeal effort in a letter penned by 12 hospital and health system leaders, many serving rural areas, though that more limited legislation passed anyway.

A repeal would harm vulnerable patients by driving up costs and thinning existing hospital staff, said Martin Chaney, CEO of Maury Regional Health, a system in rural Middle Tennessee south of Nashville. Ending the law would create rural healthcare deserts, Chaney wrote in the letter, because hospitals would choose to expand in areas that were already the most profitable, where residents had a range of health insurance providers.

“The premise that eliminating CON regulations will expand health care opportunities by increasing competition is not true for ALL Tennesseans,” Chaney wrote. “Instead, it would result in cherry-picking and increasing the gap in access to medical care in rural areas.”

A month later, TriStar Health — owned by the largest hospital company in the U.S., for-profit HCA Healthcare — applied for a certificate of need to build a hospital just 20 minutes north of Maury Regional Medical Center. Nashville-based HCA received approval despite brief opposition from Maury Regional Health, the system led by Chaney.

HCA did not respond to requests for comment.

Local leaders are divided on what the new hospital would do to healthcare in the region. “Competition is good,” Maury County Commissioner Kevin Markham told KFF Health News. Markham, like many in favor of the new hospital, said that patients should have options when it comes to choosing where they get hospital care.

But leaders of smaller hospital systems in Tennessee are worried. Judy Herbert, a Williamson County commissioner and board member at Williamson Health, another health system in the area, said ending certificate of need laws will prompt hospital closures. Big hospital systems will become the default for expensive procedures and dominate rural markets, while smaller hospitals that provided those procedures before will lose so much money, they’ll be forced to shutter or sell, Herbert reasoned, echoing the concerns of other advocates of the laws.

“Many challenges have emerged that place increasing pressure on healthcare organizations, especially independent nonprofits like Williamson Health,” that health system’s leadership said in an open letter in July 2025, citing Tennessee’s intentions around certificates of need.

In July of this year, Williamson Health’s board voted to sell its network of clinics, diagnostic centers, and a more than 330-bed hospital in a $900 million deal with Ascension St. Thomas, part of one of the largest healthcare systems in the nation.
